interest: This file is particularly valuable to historians because it captures the acute administrative, legal, and human friction surrounding dual nationality on the eve of and during World War II. It illustrates the proactive, organized efforts of tens of thousands of Japanese-Americans—most notably seen in massive Hawaiian petitions and resolutions from the Japanese American Citizens League—seeking to formally divest themselves of Japanese nationality to affirm their allegiance to the United States. Furthermore, the documents illuminate intense wartime legal debates, revealing both aggressive political efforts to strip Nisei of birthright citizenship by overturning Wong Kim Ark and the State Department's internal legal deliberations regarding the Fourteenth Amendment, wartime expatriation bans, and the diplomatic complexities of dual nationals caught between opposing belligerent states.
overview: This file contains U.S. State Department records spanning July 1940 to June 1944 concerning Japanese nationality legislation and the contested citizenship status of Japanese-Americans before and during World War II. The collection documents efforts by Nisei—particularly in the Territory of Hawaii and later in War Relocation Authority internment camps—to renounce Japanese allegiance or clarify their dual citizenship under the U.S. Nationality Act of 1940 and Japanese legal codes. It also highlights official responses, congressional inquiries, and public debates regarding birthright citizenship, wartime loyalty, and expatriation, featuring extensive legal analyses by State Department legal advisers (such as Richard W. Flournoy) on the Fourteenth Amendment, United States v. Wong Kim Ark, consular registration requirements under Japanese law, and procedures governing the repatriation and exchange of dual nationals.
